chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
title: "Wearyland Blues" with J.C. Higginbotham and how he held notes
summary: They play the Blue Note record with Higginbotham and Albert Ammons from the mid-1930s; Bunn can only credit his ear and a gift for his held notes.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: This is, "Wearyland Blues," with J. C. Higginbotham.
Uh-huh. That's me on the guitar.
Higginbotham was on the trombone, wasn't he?
Uh-huh. There's a lot of surface noise on that.
Particular record. It's a Blue Note. A lot of those Blue Note pressings were pretty cheap.
Yeah. Was that back east or out here?
Back east. That was sometime in the mid-'30s.
Those held notes, you know, the way
-- quite that style at that time.
When you first started to do that, was the idea you were thinking about the way a voice sounds?
How did you first get into doing that, that particular thing, the way you hold those notes?
I don't know. That's what's so funny, I don't know. Just a gift, I guess. And I loved music. I loved it but never could read a note. [Sure don't know] Knew how the hell that would happen.
But I got a good ear. I can hear. A tempo like this, look. A tempo like that. I hear it, got to make them changes. And I hear them, before I even get to them. "Basin Street".
